client:
I just don't see the point in doing anything anymore. Everything reminds me of Sarah - our favorite hiking trails, cooking meals, even watching TV shows we used to enjoy together. I know it's been six months, but I still wake up every morning expecting to see her there, and when she's not... it's like the air gets sucked out of the room all over again. 

I'm not sure talking about this will help - how can words change the fact that she's gone? But my friends keep pushing me to try therapy, so here I am.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're grieving Sarah, and how everything still feels so painfully fresh, like the loss is happening anew each morning. While you're uncertain if talking will help, I notice you're speaking very quickly and softly—almost like the pain is rushing out faster than words can contain it. Would it feel okay to slow down together and explore what comes up when you let yourself sit with these feelings for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if slowing down will help—when I stop talking, the silence just makes the memories louder. Sometimes it feels like if I don't keep moving or talking, the grief will swallow me whole. But I'm so tired of running from it too.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two painful places—the exhaustion of running from the grief, and the fear of what happens when you stop. Your voice has an urgent quality, like your body is bracing against the wave of emotion even as you describe wanting to rest. Could we try something different—not silence, but just breathing together for a few moments to see what that feels like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't know...when people tell me to "just breathe" it always feels so trivial, like putting a bandaid on something that needs stitches. But I am exhausted from running. It's just that stopping feels like falling backwards into something dark—like I won't be able to pull myself back out if I let go.
therapist: Your words capture that terrible dilemma so well—wanting relief from the exhaustion, but fearing the fall into darkness if you stop. I notice your voice sounds both weary and tender when you describe this, like part of you knows how much care you actually need right now, even if it feels impossible to accept simple comforts. Could we explore what "falling backwards" looks like in your mind? Sometimes naming the fear can shrink its power.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
You know, when I try to picture "falling backwards," it's not even really an image—it's more this overwhelming sense of losing control completely. Like if I let myself rest even a little, everything I've been holding together will just collapse. 

But what frustrates me is that part of me does crave that care you mentioned. I just don't trust it. It feels like a trap—like if I admit I need help, I'll become someone who always needs help. Does that make sense? I don't want to be that person.
therapist: You're describing such an important tension—yearning for care while fearing what it might mean about your strength. I hear your voice soften when you talk about that craving, like part of you is whispering that it's okay to need support, even as your words wrestle with that idea. What comes up when we consider that needing help now doesn't mean you'll always need it—that healing might actually restore your independence rather than take it away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I never thought about it that way—that needing help now could actually help me be more independent later. But part of me still worries that if I start leaning on people, I'll just become dependent and weak. It's like my brain knows logically that's not true, but my gut still tightens up at the idea of asking for support.
therapist: That tightening in your gut sounds so real—like an alarm system warning you against perceived danger, even when your rational mind knows better. I notice your voice lifts slightly when you talk about the logical side, almost like there's a glimmer of hope there. What would it feel like to acknowledge both parts—the protective gut reaction and the wiser voice that knows healing isn't weakness?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I do feel that split inside me, but the anxious part is so much louder. When I try to listen to the logical side, it's like trying to hear a whisper in a storm. And honestly, sometimes I worry that if I stop listening to the gut feeling, I'll miss some real danger—like setting the alarm system to 'off' right before a break-in.
therapist: It makes so much sense that the anxious part feels louder—it's designed to grab your attention like a fire alarm. I hear how carefully you're weighing this, your words tumbling out quickly as you describe the fear of missing real danger. What if we thought of this not as turning the alarm "off," but maybe just adjusting the sensitivity so you can also hear that quieter, wise voice when it speaks?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That makes sense in theory, but I don't know how to actually adjust the sensitivity. The anxious voice feels so automatic—like it just takes over before I can even think. And sometimes when I try to listen for that quieter voice, I just end up feeling more anxious because I can't hear it clearly.
therapist: I hear how frustrating it feels when the anxious voice drowns out the calmer one—like trying to tune a radio through static. But I notice something important: even as you describe this struggle, your voice isn't as tense as your words suggest. That tells me part of you is already practicing what we're talking about, even if it doesn't feel successful yet. Would it help to explore some specific moments when that quieter voice did break through, even just briefly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess there was one time last week when I almost canceled plans because I was spiraling, but I ended up going anyway. It still felt awful the whole time though, so I don't know if that really counts as progress. The anxiety was still there shouting at me, just quieter. 

I'm skeptical that focusing on these little moments will actually help when the big picture still feels so overwhelming. Like, what's the point of noticing a few seconds of relief when most of the time I'm drowning?
therapist: It's understandable to feel skeptical when the anxiety still feels so present, even in those moments you pushed through. But I hear something important in how you describe this—your voice softens when talking about going to the plans, like part of you recognizes that doing hard things despite the discomfort is actually quite significant. What if we hold both truths: that it still felt awful, and that you showed real strength by staying with the discomfort instead of avoiding it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I do feel a little proud that I went through with the plans, but the anxiety was so overwhelming at the time that it's hard to focus on that part. It's like my brain keeps replaying all the awkward moments and what-ifs instead of remembering that I actually survived it. I'm not sure how to hold both truths when the negative feelings are so much louder.
therapist: I notice something interesting—while you're describing how loud the negative feelings were, your voice actually carries a hint of energy and lightness when you mention feeling proud. That tells me the positive part of that experience is in there too, even if it's hard to access right now. What would it be like to revisit that moment together, not to dismiss the anxiety, but to help the pride have a little more space to breathe?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess I do remember feeling proud in that moment, but it's hard to focus on that when the anxiety comes rushing back so much stronger. Part of me worries that if I let myself feel too good about it, I'll just get disappointed when things go wrong again. 

It's like my brain keeps telling me "don't get your hopes up" even when something positive happens. I don't know how to make the good feelings stick around longer without feeling like I'm just setting myself up.
therapist: It's striking how your words express caution about disappointment, yet your voice lifts with almost a hopeful energy when you describe that moment of pride—like part of you is already practicing letting the good feeling in, even as you worry about it. Would you be willing to explore what it might look like to let that pride exist alongside the anxiety, rather than waiting for one to disappear before allowing the other?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
